By Claire Keenan Published 4 hours ago A 17-year-old girl was killed in the deadly sword attack at a high school in central Sweden on Friday, police have confirmed. Two boys aged 12 and 17 were also seriously injured in the attack at Brinell School in Fagersta, according to local authorities, while another person sustained minor injuries. An 18-year-old man was arrested but has not been identified. Police said they were treating the case as murder and attempted murder. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson visited the school, where flower tributes have been laid to honour the victims, on Saturday morning. Students at the school had only just returned to the classroom following the summer break when the deadly attack unfolded on Friday afternoon. The police later confirmed they fired shots after being called to the scene but did not say whether the alleged attacker was hit before he was detained. Sweden's public broadcaster reported that the suspect was wearing a helmet. Local media also said he was a former student. The region went into a state of emergency on Friday, but it had ended by Saturday. The school has just under 500 students on its roster, according to SVT, and is located 170km (105 miles) north-west of the capital, Stockholm. Investigators have carried out two house searches in connection with the suspect, police said. On Friday, Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson described the attack as a "serious incident," and said "we do not know what lies behind the act, but we know that police are working very intensively", in a post on X. Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf said he received the news "with dismay and sadness". It brings together journalists, media experts, and policymakers to discuss – and look for solutions – to the key challenges facing press and media freedom in Europe today. This year, the discussions will focus on the financial sustainability of journalism, growing threats in the digital space, legal harassment, foreign interference, public service media, information integrity, and gendered dimensions of attacks against journalists. We will explore how independent media can be better protected and strengthened as a cornerstone of democratic resilience and security across Europe. The project is to be based on BWRX-300 technology , a 300 MW small nuclear reactor designed as a simpler and faster-to-deploy alternative to traditional large-scale nuclear units. The reactors are expected to be built across three locations, with a total capacity of 4.2 GW, enough to power around 8 million households for at least 60 years. The total investment has been estimated at £35 billion. The United Kingdom actively encourages private investment in nuclear energy. The state remains only the regulator; it sets safety rules and designs support mechanisms, but it does not pretend that every strategic project must be run by a state-owned company. Its Advanced Nuclear Framework for Privately Led Projects was created to open the door for private investment in advanced nuclear technologies , including small modular reactors. For Poland, the contrast is uncomfortable. Sołowow has been involved in the development of SMR technology at home for several years, including through Synthos Green Energy. In Poland, however, the project is pursued together with state-owned Orlen. Łukasz Wojdyga Director of the Center for Strategic Studies Warsaw Enterprise Institute That partnership soon became a warning sign rather than a model example of public-private cooperation. The dispute centered on Orlen Synthos Green Energy, the joint venture created by Orlen and Synthos Green Energy. According to media reports, tensions grew over who would actually control the project, how far Orlen would remain involved, who would carry the risks, and who would benefit from access to the technology. What was supposed to be a strategic partnership increasingly looked like a rivalry between a state-controlled giant and a private investor. The case was later reviewed by the prosecutor’s office, including administrative decisions related to the project and earlier concerns raised by security services. The proceedings were ultimately discontinued. But the damage to trust between the partners had already been done. The project became another example of how difficult it can be in Poland to combine private capital with state-controlled structures in sectors considered “strategic.” Related Posts US Greenland Deal: Does America Now Control Greenland? Hormuz Needs a Community, Not a Condominium Russia Near Poland’s Border: Less Talk, More Deterrence Georgia’s FIntech Push Needs Authority Budgets For AI Agents This is Poland’s bad habit, that strategic projects are still too often expected to pass through state-owned companies or remain under strong political supervision. In practice, this means that private investors may bring money and know-how, but the state still wants to keep the steering wheel. Poland needs stable, low-emission energy if it wants to keep industry competitive, attract data centers, develop advanced technologies, and prevent production from moving abroad. Renewables will play an important role, but they require grid expansion, storage, and balancing capacity. Nuclear power, including smaller reactors, can provide reliable electricity regardless of weather conditions. Small modular reactors are not a magic fix. They still require licensing, financing, locations, public acceptance, and strict oversight. But none of that means the state has to dominate every project. The state should set clear rules, protect safety, and issue decisions efficiently. It should not turn every strategic investment into a test of alignment with state-controlled companies. If Poland fails to create room for private investors in strategic sectors, it should not be surprised when Polish capital builds the future elsewhere. The market is not the obstacle here. The obstacle is a state that still too often confuses national interest with state ownership.
